title: GitHub Workflows
description: A practical reference for building CI/CD pipelines with GitHub Actions: workflow syntax, triggers, jobs, reusable workflows, and common recipes.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
GitHub Actions workflows are YAML files stored in `.github/workflows/` at the
root of your repository. Each file defines one workflow: what triggers it,
what jobs it runs, and what steps each job executes.

## 1. Create your first workflow

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run a script
        run: echo "Hello from Actions"
```

Commit and push this file. GitHub picks it up automatically — no separate
registration step is needed.

## 2. Where to see it run

Open your repository on GitHub and click the **Actions** tab. Every push or
pull request matching the `on:` triggers above creates a new workflow run,
with one row per job and expandable logs per step.

## 3. Core building blocks

- **Workflow** — the whole YAML file; identified by `name:`.
- **Event (`on:`)** — what causes the workflow to run (push, pull request, schedule, manual dispatch, etc.). See [Triggers](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/triggers/).
- **Job** — a set of steps that run on the same runner. Jobs run in parallel by default. See [Jobs and Runners](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/jobs-and-runners/).
- **Step** — a single command (`run:`) or a packaged action (`uses:`).
- **Action** — reusable packaged step, either from the [Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace?type=actions), a public repo, or your own. See [Using Actions](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/using-actions/).

## 4. Next steps

- [Triggers](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/triggers/) — every way to start a workflow.
- [Jobs and Runners](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/jobs-and-runners/) — dependencies, matrices, runner choice.
- [Environment Variables and Secrets](/github-workflows/0.0.0/getting-started/environment-variables-and-secrets/) — configuration and credentials.
Getting Started.Workflow Syntax Basics:
Every workflow file follows the same top-level shape. This page covers the
pieces you'll touch in nearly every workflow.

## Top-level keys

```yaml
name: CI
run-name: CI run for ${{ github.actor }}

on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  NODE_ENV: production

jobs:
  # ...
```

| Key | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Display name shown in the Actions tab. Optional; defaults to the file path. |
| `run-name` | Dynamic per-run title, supports expressions. |
| `on` | Trigger(s) for the workflow. |
| `permissions` | Default `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions for all jobs. |
| `env` | Environment variables available to every job/step. |
| `jobs` | One or more named jobs (required). |

## Steps

A step is either a shell command or an action:

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Print Dart version
    run: dart --version

  - name: Checkout code
    uses: actions/checkout@v4
    with:
      fetch-depth: 0
```

- `run:` executes shell commands (`bash` on Linux/macOS runners, `pwsh` on Windows by default).
- `uses:` references an action, pinned to a tag, branch, or full commit SHA.
- `with:` passes named inputs to an action.
- `id:` names a step so later steps can read its `outputs`.

## Expressions and contexts

Double-curly syntax `${{ ... }}` evaluates expressions against contexts like
`github`, `env`, `secrets`, `matrix`, and `steps`:

```yaml
- name: Use a previous step's output
  run: echo "Built version is ${{ steps.version.outputs.value }}"

- name: Conditional step
  if: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
  run: echo "On main"
```

See the official [contexts reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/contexts)
for the full list of available contexts.

## YAML gotchas

- Indentation is significant; use spaces, not tabs.
- Quote strings that start with a special character, e.g. `on: "push"` is rarely needed, but `if: "contains(...)"` sometimes is when the expression starts with a brace-like token.
- Multiline `run:` blocks use `|` (preserve newlines) or `>` (fold into one line):

```yaml
- run: |
    echo "line one"
    echo "line two"
```
Getting Started.Environment Variables and Secrets:
Workflows need configuration (environment variables) and credentials
(secrets), scoped at the workflow, job, or step level.

## Environment variables

Defined at any of three levels; step-level overrides job-level overrides
workflow-level:

```yaml
env:
  GLOBAL_VAR: workflow-level

jobs:
  build:
    env:
      JOB_VAR: job-level
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "$GLOBAL_VAR $JOB_VAR $STEP_VAR"
        env:
          STEP_VAR: step-level
```

Default variables GitHub provides automatically (a few of the most used):

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` | `owner/repo` |
| `GITHUB_SHA` | Commit SHA that triggered the run |
| `GITHUB_REF` | Ref that triggered the run, e.g. `refs/heads/main` |
| `GITHUB_WORKSPACE` | Absolute path to the checked-out repo on the runner |
| `RUNNER_OS` | `Linux`, `Windows`, or `macOS` |

Full list: [default environment variables](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/variables#default-environment-variables).

## Secrets

Secrets are set in **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions** on the
repository, environment, or organization. They're never printed in logs
(GitHub redacts matching values automatically).

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Deploy
    env:
      API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
    run: ./deploy.sh
```

- Secrets aren't passed to workflows triggered by pull requests from forks,
  for security reasons — see [Security Hardening](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/security-hardening/).
- Repository, environment, and organization secrets can all coexist; a job
  tied to an `environment:` gets that environment's secrets too.

## Repository and organization variables

Non-secret configuration can live in **Variables** (same settings page) and
is referenced via the `vars` context:

```yaml
- run: echo "Deploying to ${{ vars.DEPLOY_REGION }}"
```

Use variables for non-sensitive config that changes per environment (regions,
feature flags); use secrets for anything sensitive (tokens, keys,
credentials).

Guides.Triggers:
The `on:` key controls when a workflow runs. It accepts a single event, a
list of events, or a map of events with filters.

## Common triggers

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, "release/**"]
    tags: ["v*"]
    paths: ["src/**", "!src/**/*.md"]

  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

  schedule:
    - cron: "0 3 * * *"   # 03:00 UTC daily

  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: "Target environment"
        required: true
        default: "staging"
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]

  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      version:
        required: true
        type: string
```

| Trigger | Fires on |
| --- | --- |
| `push` | Commits pushed to matching branches/tags. |
| `pull_request` | PR opened/updated against matching base branches. |
| `schedule` | Cron schedule, UTC only. |
| `workflow_dispatch` | Manual "Run workflow" button, with optional typed inputs. |
| `workflow_call` | Makes the workflow reusable/callable from another workflow. |
| `release` | A release is published/created/edited. |
| `issues`, `issue_comment` | Issue or comment activity — useful for chatops-style automation. |

## Filtering

- `branches` / `branches-ignore` — mutually exclusive glob filters on branch name.
- `paths` / `paths-ignore` — only run when matching files changed (`push`/`pull_request` only).
- `tags` / `tags-ignore` — same idea for tag pushes.

Filters use glob syntax, not regex: `"release/**"` matches any nesting under
`release/`, `"v*"` matches `v1`, `v2.0.0`, etc.

## Manual dispatch inputs

`workflow_dispatch` inputs show up as form fields in the Actions UI and are
available via `github.event.inputs.<name>`:

```yaml
steps:
  - run: echo "Deploying to ${{ github.event.inputs.environment }}"
```

## Concurrency

Prevent overlapping runs (e.g. cancel an in-progress deploy when a new one is
pushed):

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: deploy-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```
Guides.Jobs and Runners:
Jobs are the unit of parallelism. By default every job in a workflow runs
concurrently on a fresh runner; use `needs:` to sequence them.

## Choosing a runner

```yaml
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest   # also: windows-latest, macos-latest, or self-hosted labels
```

GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral VMs with common toolchains preinstalled
(see the [runner images](https://github.com/actions/runner-images) repo for
exact package lists per OS).

## Job dependencies

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]

  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]

  deploy:
    needs: [test, build]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]
```

`deploy` only runs once both `test` and `build` succeed. Use `if:` with
`needs.<job>.result` to run on failure too (e.g. a notification job):

```yaml
  notify:
    needs: [test, build]
    if: always() && (needs.test.result == 'failure' || needs.build.result == 'failure')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Something failed"
```

## Matrix builds

Run the same job across a grid of variables — the most common use is testing
multiple language/SDK versions or OSes in parallel:

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        dart-version: ["3.5", "3.6", "stable"]
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
      fail-fast: false
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with:
          sdk: ${{ matrix.dart-version }}
      - run: dart test
```

This produces one job per combination (6 jobs above). `fail-fast: false`
keeps all combinations running even if one fails; `max-parallel` caps how
many run at once.

## Passing data between jobs

Jobs don't share filesystem state, so pass data via `outputs` + `needs`, or
via [artifacts](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/artifacts-and-caching/) for files:

```yaml
jobs:
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      value: ${{ steps.get_version.outputs.value }}
    steps:
      - id: get_version
        run: echo "value=1.2.3" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  build:
    needs: version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Building version ${{ needs.version.outputs.value }}"
```
Guides.Using Actions:
Actions are reusable units of workflow logic, referenced with `uses:`. They
come from the [Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace?type=actions), any
public GitHub repo, or your own repo/organization.

## Referencing an action

```yaml
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4          # tag (recommended for readability)
  - uses: actions/checkout@main        # branch (moves; avoid for anything but experimentation)
  - uses: actions/checkout@8f4b7f8...  # full commit SHA (most secure, immutable)
  - uses: ./.github/actions/my-action  # local action in the same repo
```

Pinning to a full commit SHA is the safest option for third-party actions
since tags can be moved; see [Security Hardening](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/security-hardening/).

## Commonly used actions

| Action | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `actions/checkout` | Clone the repository onto the runner. |
| `actions/setup-node`, `actions/setup-python`, `dart-lang/setup-dart` | Install a language toolchain. |
| `actions/cache` | Cache dependencies between runs. |
| `actions/upload-artifact` / `actions/download-artifact` | Pass files between jobs or out of a run. |
| `actions/github-script` | Run arbitrary JS with an authenticated Octokit client. |
| `softprops/action-gh-release` | Create a GitHub Release with attached files. |

## Writing your own composite action

A composite action bundles multiple steps into one reusable `uses:` entry.
Create `.github/actions/setup-project/action.yml`:

```yaml
name: "Setup project"
description: "Checkout and install Dart dependencies"
runs:
  using: "composite"
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
    - run: dart pub get
      shell: bash
```

Use it like any other action:

```yaml
steps:
  - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-project
```

## Reusable workflows vs. composite actions

- **Composite action** — a reusable set of *steps*, invoked with `uses:` inside a job.
- **Reusable workflow** — a reusable set of *jobs*, invoked with `uses:` at the job level via `workflow_call`. See [Reusable Workflows](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/reusable-workflows/).

Use a composite action for a small chunk of steps shared across jobs; use a
reusable workflow when you want to share entire job structures (matrices,
multiple jobs, `needs` graphs) across repositories.
Guides.Reusable Workflows:
A reusable workflow is a normal workflow file that declares `workflow_call`
as a trigger, letting other workflows invoke it as a single job step.

## Defining a reusable workflow

```yaml
# .github/workflows/reusable-build.yml
name: Reusable Build

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      dart-version:
        required: false
        type: string
        default: "stable"
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN:
        required: false
    outputs:
      artifact-name:
        description: "Name of the uploaded build artifact"
        value: ${{ jobs.build.outputs.artifact-name }}

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      artifact-name: build-output
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with:
          sdk: ${{ inputs.dart-version }}
      - run: dart pub get
      - run: dart compile exe bin/main.dart -o build/app
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: build-output
          path: build/app
```

## Calling it

From another workflow in the same repo, or any repo that can access it:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  call-build:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-build.yml
    with:
      dart-version: "3.6"
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
```

Cross-repository reuse works the same way with a full reference:

```yaml
jobs:
  call-build:
    uses: my-org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/reusable-build.yml@v1
```

## Rules and limits

- Secrets are **not** inherited automatically — pass them explicitly with
  `secrets:`, or use `secrets: inherit` to forward everything from the caller.
- A reusable workflow can itself call other reusable workflows, up to a
  nesting depth GitHub enforces (currently 4 levels).
- `env:` set in the caller is **not** visible inside the called workflow;
  pass configuration through `with:` inputs instead.
Guides.Artifacts and Caching:
Artifacts persist files produced by a run (for download or handoff between
jobs); caching speeds up repeated runs by reusing dependency downloads/builds.

## Artifacts

```yaml
- name: Upload build output
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: app-binary
    path: build/app
    retention-days: 7

- name: Download in a later job
  uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: app-binary
    path: ./downloaded
```

Artifacts are visible in the run summary UI for download and are the
standard way to move build output from a `build` job to a `deploy` job that
runs on a different runner.

## Caching

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: |
      ~/.pub-cache
      .dart_tool
    key: pub-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('pubspec.lock') }}
    restore-keys: |
      pub-${{ runner.os }}-
```

- `key` should include a hash of the lockfile so the cache invalidates when
  dependencies change.
- `restore-keys` provides fallbacks: a partial-match cache is still faster
  than none.
- Some setup actions (e.g. `actions/setup-node` with `cache: npm`) wrap
  `actions/cache` internally — check the action's docs before adding a
  manual cache step on top.

## Artifacts vs. caching

| | Artifacts | Cache |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Output you want to keep/inspect/deploy | Speeding up future runs |
| Lifetime | Configurable retention (default 90 days) | Evicted automatically (LRU, ~10 GB per repo) |
| Typical content | Binaries, test reports, logs | Package manager directories, build intermediates |
Guides.Security Hardening:
Workflows execute arbitrary code with access to repository contents and
whatever secrets you grant them, so a few defaults matter.

## Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA

```yaml
# Less safe: tag can be moved by the action's maintainer (or an attacker who compromises their account)
- uses: some-org/some-action@v2

# Safer: immutable reference
- uses: some-org/some-action@8f4b7f8c2b1e4a9d6c3f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d
```

Dependabot can keep pinned SHAs up to date automatically if you enable
updates for `github-actions` in `dependabot.yml`.

## Least-privilege `GITHUB_TOKEN`

Set restrictive default permissions and grant more only where needed:

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  release:
    permissions:
      contents: write   # only this job can create releases/tags
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]
```

## Be careful with `pull_request_target` and fork PRs

- `pull_request` from a fork runs with a read-only token and **no access to
  secrets** — this is the safe default for untrusted code.
- `pull_request_target` runs with the base repo's permissions and secrets,
  even for fork PRs — only use it when you do not check out or execute the
  fork's code, or you've explicitly reviewed it first.

## Avoid script injection via untrusted input

Never interpolate untrusted values (PR titles, issue bodies, branch names)
directly into a `run:` shell string:

```yaml
# Unsafe: title could contain shell metacharacters
- run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

# Safer: pass through an environment variable
- env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "$TITLE"
```

The environment-variable form avoids the value ever being interpreted as
shell syntax.

Reference for the YAML keys available in a workflow file, grouped by
where they can appear.

## Top level

| Key | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | Workflow display name. |
| `run-name` | string | Per-run display name; supports expressions. |
| `on` | string / list / map | Trigger configuration. |
| `permissions` | string / map | Default `GITHUB_TOKEN` scopes. |
| `env` | map | Workflow-wide environment variables. |
| `defaults` | map | Default `run:` shell/working-directory for all jobs. |
| `concurrency` | map | Deduplicate/cancel overlapping runs. |
| `jobs` | map | Required; one entry per job. |

## Job level

| Key | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `runs-on` | string / list | Runner label(s). |
| `needs` | string / list | Jobs that must complete first. |
| `if` | expression | Conditional execution. |
| `strategy` | map | `matrix`, `fail-fast`, `max-parallel`. |
| `env` | map | Job-level environment variables. |

| `timeout-minutes` | number | Kill the job if it exceeds this duration. |

| Key | Type | Notes |

API Reference.Contexts:
Contexts are objects available inside `${{ ... }}` expressions, giving
access to run metadata, inputs, and results of previous steps/jobs.

| Context | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `github` | `github.repository`, `github.sha`, `github.event_name`, `github.actor` | Info about the workflow run and triggering event. |
| `env` | `env.MY_VAR` | Variables set via `env:`. |
| `vars` | `vars.DEPLOY_REGION` | Configuration variables (non-secret). |
| `secrets` | `secrets.API_TOKEN` | Secrets available to the job. |
| `job` | `job.status` | Status of the current job so far. |
| `steps` | `steps.<id>.outputs.<name>`, `steps.<id>.outcome` | Outputs/results of previous steps in the same job. |
| `runner` | `runner.os`, `runner.temp` | Info about the runner executing the job. |
| `needs` | `needs.<job>.outputs.<name>`, `needs.<job>.result` | Outputs/results of jobs this job depends on. |
| `matrix` | `matrix.os`, `matrix.dart-version` | Current combination in a matrix strategy. |
| `inputs` | `inputs.<name>` | Inputs for `workflow_dispatch` or `workflow_call`. |
| `strategy` | `strategy.job-index` | Metadata about the current matrix strategy. |

## Reading event payload data

The full webhook payload that triggered the run is under `github.event`:

```yaml
- run: echo "PR number is ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}"
  if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
```

The shape of `github.event` matches the corresponding [webhook event payload](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads).

## Step outputs

A step exposes outputs by writing to the `GITHUB_OUTPUT` file:

```yaml
- id: info
  run: echo "sha_short=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
- run: echo "Short SHA is ${{ steps.info.outputs.sha_short }}"
```
API Reference.Expression Functions:
Built-in functions usable inside `${{ ... }}` expressions.

## String and collection functions

| Function | Example | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `contains(haystack, needle)` | `contains(github.ref, 'refs/tags/')` | `true`/`false` |
| `startsWith(str, prefix)` | `startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/heads/')` | `true`/`false` |
| `endsWith(str, suffix)` | `endsWith(matrix.os, 'latest')` | `true`/`false` |
| `format(str, ...args)` | `format('Hello {0}', github.actor)` | `"Hello octocat"` |
| `join(array, sep)` | `join(fromJSON('["a","b"]'), ', ')` | `"a, b"` |
| `toJSON(value)` | `toJSON(github.event)` | JSON string |
| `fromJSON(str)` | `fromJSON(needs.setup.outputs.matrix)` | parsed value |

## Status check functions

Used in `if:` to control a step/job's behavior relative to prior failures —
by default, a step is skipped once any previous step in the job has failed.

| Function | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `success()` | True if no previous step has failed (the default condition). |
| `always()` | Always true, even after a failure or cancellation — for cleanup/notification steps. |
| `failure()` | True if any previous step in the job has failed. |
| `cancelled()` | True if the run was cancelled. |

```yaml
- name: Notify on failure
  if: failure()
  run: ./notify.sh "build failed"

- name: Always clean up
  if: always()
  run: ./cleanup.sh
```

## Operators

Expressions support `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, `||`, `!`, and
parentheses for grouping, e.g.:

```yaml
if: ${{ (github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main') || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' }}
```

Project.FAQ:
### Why didn't my workflow trigger?

Common causes: the YAML is invalid (check the Actions tab for a parse error
banner), the file isn't in `.github/workflows/`, the `on:` filters
(`branches`, `paths`) don't match the push/PR, or the workflow file itself
was added in the same commit/branch that should trigger it — new workflow
files are only picked up once they exist on the default branch for some
trigger types.

### Why can't my job see a secret?

Secrets aren't passed to workflows triggered by `pull_request` from a forked
repository, by design. Also check the secret is defined at the right scope
(repository, environment, or org) and that the job's `environment:` matches
if it's an environment secret.

### How do I debug a failing step without re-running everything?

Enable step debug logging by setting the repository secret
`ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG` to `true`, or use `tmate`-based actions
(`mxschmitt/action-tmate`) to get an interactive SSH session into the runner
mid-job for local debugging.

### Can I run a workflow only when specific files change?

Yes — use `paths:`/`paths-ignore:` under `push`/`pull_request`. Note this
filtering does not apply to `workflow_dispatch` or `schedule` triggers.

### How do I stop a stale workflow run when I push again?

Use a `concurrency:` group keyed on the ref, with `cancel-in-progress: true`.
See [Triggers](/github-workflows/0.0.0/guides/triggers/).

### Where do I see cron trigger runs if nothing seems to happen?

`schedule` runs are suppressed on repositories with no activity for 60 days,
and cron times are approximate (queued, not guaranteed to the minute) during
periods of high GitHub Actions load.

## Style conventions used in these docs

- Code fences always include a language hint (` ```yaml `, ` ```bash `).
- Every YAML example is meant to be copy-pasteable and minimal — trimmed to
  just the keys relevant to the topic at hand, not a full real-world
  workflow.
